Diffusive time scale (tD​∼L2/κ)

Words: 47
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
A concentration varying over length L has Laplacian of order its amplitude divided by L2. Balancing the time derivative with κΔχ in the diffusion equation gives the displayed relaxation time. A multiple-scale expansion with spatial scale εx therefore uses slow time ε2t when the effective diffusivity is of order one.

Variable-coefficient conservative diffusion equation (ut​=(a(x)ux​)x​)

Words: 57
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
With positive diffusion coefficient a(x), this diffusion equation expresses conservation with flux −a(x)ux​. For a differentiable coefficient, its spatial operator is auxx​+a′ux​, rather than either aux​ or auxx​ alone. A symmetric half-grid diffusion consistency discretization uses the difference of the two adjacent interface fluxes, preserving that divergence structure. Suitable Dirichlet boundary conditions make the spatial operator dissipative in the L2 norm.

Infinite propagation speed

Words: 50
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
Infinite propagation speed means that a disturbance initially confined to a bounded region can affect arbitrarily distant points after any positive time. The strictly positive heat kernel gives this behavior for a nontrivial nonnegative diffusion solution. It contrasts with the finite propagation speed of the wave equation; a very small distant response is still mathematically nonzero.

Periodic homogenization of a diffusion equation

Words: 29
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
For ut​=∂x​[a(x/ϵ)ux​] with positive periodic a, the one-dimensional homogenized diffusivity is the harmonic mean aeff​=⟨a−1⟩−1. Microscopic flux continuity produces this harmonic rather than arithmetic averaging.

Porous medium equation (ut​=Δ(um))

Words: 585 Articles: 10
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
The porous medium equation ut​=Δ(um) with m>1 is a nonlinear partial differential equation whose diffusivity vanishes at u=0. Unlike the heat equation, it has compactly supported solutions with finite propagation speed.

Integrating the similarity equation once gives ff′=−ξf/5, and normalization ∫0∞​ξ2fdξ=1 fixes the compact-support radius. The flux vanishes at the moving front, so the profile solves the equation weakly and approaches the prescribed point mass as time tends to zero.

Substitution reduces the equation to (ξF2F′)′=−(ξ2F)′ when λ5λ˙=D0​/r02​. Zero central flux and F(0)=1 give the compact profile shown above, with λ6=6D0​t/r02​. Finite propagation in porous-medium diffusion

Words: 58
Porous medium equation OurBigBook.com
In a porous medium equation with exponent m>1, the effective diffusion coefficient vanishes at zero density. A nonnegative compactly supported source profile can therefore retain a finite front for every finite positive time. For example, the radial cubic-diffusion source profile has support radius proportional to t1/6. This notion concerns a moving diffusion front; it does not require the constant characteristic cone used for a wave equation.

Forced filling similarity for power-law diffusion

Words: 74
Porous medium equation OurBigBook.com
Consider a nonlinear diffusion equation with uniform supply, ϕht​=Dm​(hmhx​)x​+R, on x>0, with an absorbing boundary h(0,t)=0 and initially h=0. Far from the boundary, h=Rt/ϕ. Balancing the time derivative, supply, and diffusion gives
h=ϕRt​F(η),η=ℓ(t)x​,ℓ(t)=[ϕm+1Dm​Rmtm+1​]1/2.
(1)
The similarity solution satisfies
(FmF′)′+1−F+2m+1​ηF′=0,F(0)=0,F(∞)=1.
(2)
The outward boundary volume flux per unit width is Q=Rℓcm​, where cm​=limη↓0​FmF′. Integrating the equation gives
cm​=2m+3​∫0∞​(1−F)dη.
(3)
Thus the growing region of depleted storage fixes the discharge prefactor, and Q∝t(m+1)/2.

Porous medium equation OurBigBook.com
For ϕht​=Dm​(hmhx​)x​ on 0<x<L, with h(0,t)=0 and zero right-hand volume flux, a separation of variables gives
h=(mDm​τϕL2​)1/mF(x/L),τ=t+t0​,
(4)
where the positive profile satisfies
(FmF′)′+F=0,F(0)=0,F′(1)=0.
(5)
Its boundary volume flux per unit width is
Q=LDm​​(mDm​τϕL2​)(m+1)/mcm​,cm​=limξ↓0​FmF′=∫01​Fdξ.
(6)
These profiles are exact separated solutions and describe the leading long-time discharge for a broad class of positive initial data. The virtual origin t0​ depends on the initial profile; it does not make the separated solution an exact representation of every initial condition.

Reaction-diffusion spectral decay threshold (κ<π2,κh​=4h−2sin2(πh/2))

Words: 73
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
On the unit interval with zero Dirichlet boundary conditions, ut​=uxx​+κu has sine-mode growth rates κ−j2π2. Every finite-energy initial condition decays exactly when the largest rate is negative, namely κ<π2. A centered finite difference grid with h=1/(M+1) has eigenvectors sin(jπm/(M+1)) and growth rates κ−4h−2sin2(jπ/(2(M+1))). Its all-data decay threshold is the displayed κh​, strictly less than π2 and approaching it from below. Equality leaves a stationary lowest mode; exceeding the threshold allows growth.

Heat evolution of bounded data need not converge at large times

Words: 63
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
Bounded smooth initial data alone do not guarantee a pointwise large-time limit for the heat equation on Euclidean space. In four dimensions, g(x)=(1+∣x∣2)i has modulus one. At the origin its heat kernel average is asymptotic to 4iΓ(2+i)ti, which oscillates indefinitely. Initial data vanishing at infinity do have heat averages tending to zero. This distinction matters when using Duhamel principle to construct a stationary solution for a time-independent source.

Dirichlet heat-reaction threshold on the unit square (κ≤2π2)

Words: 80
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
For zero Dirichlet boundary conditions on the unit square, the modes 2sin(jπx)sin(kπy) have heat-reaction growth rates κ−π2(j2+k2). Their largest rate is κ−2π2. Hence the solution is an L2 norm contraction for κ≤2π2 and decays uniformly at positive times as t→∞ when the inequality is strict. At equality the first sine mode is stationary. For larger fixed κ the equation remains well posed on every finite time interval, but has a growing mode; long-time contractivity is a different property from finite-time well-posedness.

Heat operator (L=∂t​−Δ)

Words: 37
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
For the sign convention Δ=div∇, the heat operator is the differential operator L=∂t​−Δ. The heat equation is Lu=0. If P=−Δ is the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator, the same operator is ∂t​+P. A Riemannian heat kernel is a fundamental solution with the initial Dirac delta distribution.

Heat-equation uniqueness under Gaussian growth (∣u(x,t)∣≤Mea∣x∣2)

Words: 85
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
Classical heat equation solutions with identical continuous initial data and a uniform Gaussian spatial growth bound on each finite time interval are unique. For the zero-data difference, choose b>a and compare on a short slab with εΦb​, where Φb​=(1−4bt)−n/2exp(b∣x∣2/(1−4bt)) solves the equation for t<1/(4b). Its faster spatial growth controls the lateral boundary of large cylinders. The heat equation maximum principle bounds both signs of the difference by εΦb​ inside. Increasing the cylinder radius and then sending ε to zero proves uniqueness on that slab; repeating slabs covers the finite interval.

Backward heat equation (ut​=−Duxx​,D>0)

Words: 128 Articles: 1
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
A Fourier mode has multiplier eDk2t, amplifying arbitrarily small high-frequency data. For a fixed positive time t0​, initial modes e−Dn2t0​/2sin(nx) tend to zero in L2 while their values at t0​ grow without bound. This violates continuous dependence on initial data and gives an ill-posed problem in ordinary unweighted spaces. An analytic-data restriction or physical short-scale regularization changes that conclusion.

Space-time harmonic functions along Brownian motion (ft​+21​fxx​=0)

Words: 76
Backward heat equation OurBigBook.com
For f∈C2(R2) and standard Brownian motion B, the drift in Itô formula for f(Bt​,t) vanishes exactly when the displayed equation holds for every spatial point and every t≥0. Necessity follows because a zero finite-variation integral has continuous integrand ft​(Bt​,t)+21​fxx​(Bt​,t) equal to zero, and at every positive time the normal distribution of Bt​ has full support. Continuity extends the equation to time zero. There is no condition at negative times except compatibility with the global smoothness of f.

Heat equation maximum principle

Words: 54
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
On a closed manifold with a Riemannian metric, the minimum of a smooth heat solution cannot fall below its initial minimum. At a spatial minimum, Δu≤0 for the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator. Adding a small increasing function of time and considering the first crossing gives the assertion. Applying the result to nonnegative initial functions shows that the Riemannian heat kernel is nonnegative.

Heat equation energy identity (dtd​∥u∥22​=−2∥du∥22​)

Words: 34
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
On a closed manifold with a Riemannian metric, a smooth solution of ∂t​u+Δu=0 for the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator satisfies the displayed identity by integration by parts. Zero initial data force the solution to vanish, proving uniqueness and the semigroup property for heat evolution.

w(x,t)=∫0L​K(x,y,t)w0​(y)dy+∫0t​[Ky​(x,0,t−s)g(s)−Ky​(x,L,t−s)h(s)]ds.

Half-line drift boundary kernel (Pα​(x,t)=2π​t3/2x​e−(x+αt)2/(4t))

Words: 64
Dirichlet boundary-forcing heat-kernel formula OurBigBook.com
Convolution of this kernel with Dirichlet boundary data supplies the boundary forcing for ut​=uxx​+αux​ on x>0. It is −(2∂x​+α)H(x+αt,t). For α≥0, its total time mass is e−αx, tending to one as x↓0, and its mass away from zero time tends to zero. Thus the boundary value is recovered through an approximate identity, not by pointwise substitution x=0 in the kernel.

Dirichlet energy dissipation for the heat equation

Words: 59
Heat equation OurBigBook.com
For a real smooth solution wt​=Δw on a bounded regular domain with wt​=0 on its boundary, differentiation and Green's first identity yield
dtd​∫V​∣∇w∣2dV=−2∫V​(Δw)2dV≤0.
(13)
The boundary term is zero because the boundary values are fixed in time, not because the normal derivative vanishes. Equality at a particular time is equivalent to Δw=0 throughout the domain at that time.

Heat kernel trace formula (Tre−tΔ=∫M​Kt​(x,x)dvolg​(x))

Words: 66
Heat kernel OurBigBook.com
On a closed manifold, the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator has a smooth heat kernel and its heat semigroup is a trace-class operator for positive time. Expanding in a smooth orthonormal eigenbasis gives Kt​(x,y)=∑j​e−tλj​ϕj​(x)ϕj​(y)​. Elliptic regularity bounds each derivative of ϕj​ polynomially in λj​, while the exponential dominates those powers, so the expansion converges with all derivatives. Integrating the diagonal and using the unit norm of each eigenfunction proves the formula. For a bundle operator, insert the fibre matrix trace inside the integral.

Positive diffusivity requirement for the forward heat kernel (εz>0)

Words: 55
Heat kernel OurBigBook.com
The real Gaussian function heat kernel (4πεz)−1/2exp[−(ϕ−θ)2/(4εz)] is integrable only when εz>0. For forward time z>0, this requires positive diffusivity. A Cole-Hopf transformation is an algebraic substitution for any nonzero coefficient, but that does not make the real forward convolution valid for negative diffusivity. Constant initial heat data already produce a divergent integral with the wrong sign.

Heat-kernel convolution (u(⋅,t)=Kt​∗g)

Words: 48
Heat kernel OurBigBook.com
For the heat equation on Rn with diffusion coefficient one, the heat kernel is Kt​(x)=(4πt)−n/2e−∣x∣2/(4t). Its convolution with bounded initial data is smooth for positive time, solves the equation by differentiation under the integral, and returns continuous initial data locally uniformly through the approximate identity property. It is Gaussian filtering with per-coordinate variance 2t.

Riemannian heat kernel (H(t,x,y))

Words: 404 Articles: 6
Heat kernel OurBigBook.com
For the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator, the kernel solving (∂t​+Δx​)H=0 with initial Dirac delta distribution on the diagonal represents the heat semigroup. On a closed manifold with a Riemannian metric it is smooth for t>0, symmetric, nonnegative, preserves constants, and obeys the semigroup property.
Heat kernel on a finite isometric quotient (KU\N​(t,xˉ,yˉ​)=∑u∈U​KN​(t,x,uy))
Words: 161 Articles: 1
Riemannian heat kernel OurBigBook.com
For a finite free action by Riemannian isometries, the Riemannian heat kernel on the quotient is the image sum shown above. Integrating over a fundamental domain combines all images into the integral on the covering manifold, proving the initial condition and showing that there is no averaging factor in the kernel. The heat trace does have an averaging factor 1/∣U∣, because the integral of a quotient function over the cover is ∣U∣ times its quotient integral. Mere freeness of a general nondiscrete group action is not enough for this covering formula.
Heat semigroup descent through a finite normal covering (Iϕ=∣U∣−1/2ϕ∘p)
Words: 75
Heat kernel on a finite isometric quotient OurBigBook.com
The normalized pullback is a unitary map from L2 of the quotient onto the deck-invariant subspace of L2 of the cover. Local isometry and the sheet-counting integration formula preserve the Dirichlet quadratic form. Therefore the Friedrichs extension and its heat semigroup intertwine with this map. A finite sum of lifted Riemannian heat kernels gives the quotient kernel; independence of lifts follows by reindexing the deck group. This formulation avoids a uniqueness claim for unrestricted heat-equation solutions on a noncompact or incomplete manifold.
Spectral expansion of the Riemannian heat kernel (H(t,x,y)=∑j​e−tλj​ϕj​(x)ϕj​(y)​)
Words: 39
Riemannian heat kernel OurBigBook.com
On a closed manifold with a Riemannian metric, an orthonormal eigenbasis for the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator gives this formula, with eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. Polynomial elliptic bounds and exponential time decay give convergence of every derivative away from time zero. The conjugate is necessary for a complex basis.

An approximate Riemannian heat kernel with the correct delta initial limit and a residual extending with enough regularity to time zero. Reaction–diffusion system

Words: 1k Articles: 29
Diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
A reaction-diffusion system combines local reaction kinetics with spatial diffusion,
ut​=DΔu+f(u).
(47)

Bistable cubic reaction-diffusion equation (ut​=Duxx​+u(1−u)(u−r))

Words: 143 Articles: 1
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
The scalar equation ut​=Duxx​+u(1−u)(u−r) with D>0 and 0<r<1 has two stable homogeneous phases u=0,1 and an unstable intervening equilibrium u=r. Indeed the reaction derivatives at these three equilibria are −r, −(1−r) and r(1−r), respectively. A travelling wave can connect the two stable phases. At the equal-depth value r=1/2, its decreasing heteroclinic orbit is stationary. Away from this value the phases have unequal potential depths and the front propagates.

Logistic front of a bistable cubic equation (U=[1+e(x−ct−q0​)/2D​]−1)

Words: 75
Bistable cubic reaction-diffusion equation OurBigBook.com
For the decreasing front connecting 1 to 0, the balanced stationary travelling-wave reduction of a reaction-diffusion system has first integral DUx2​/2−U2(1−U)2/4=0. Choosing the negative derivative gives Ux​=−U(1−U)/2D​ and hence U=[1+e(x−q)/2D​]−1. This logistic profile remains an exact travelling wave when the reaction parameter differs from 1/2: using z=(x−ct−q0​)/D​, its derivative is Uz​=−U(1−U)/2​, and the wave equation is satisfied for c=D/2​(1−2r). Thus the speed changes with the potential bias while the shape, apart from translation, does not.

Basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model ((u∗​,v∗​)=(1+r,(1+r)2))

Words: 313 Articles: 2
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
A quadratic activator can have both basal production and activation inhibited by a second species. A normalized example has reaction rates f(u,v)=1+ru2/v−u and g(u,v)=q(u2−v), with r,q>0 and positive concentrations. At its spatially homogeneous equilibrium, v=u2, so u∗​=1+r and v∗​=(1+r)2. Writing a=(r−1)/(r+1), its reaction Jacobian matrix is J=(a2q(1+r)​−r/(1+r)2−q​). Thus trJ=a−q and detJ=q>0, giving linear asymptotic stability when q>a and instability when q<a. Basal production makes a change sign at r=1; a positive activation feedback needed for a conventional Turing instability requires r>1.

Weak focus at the Hopf threshold of a basal activator-inhibitor model (ℓ1​=(a−1)/8<0)

Words: 142
Basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model OurBigBook.com
At q=a=(r−1)/(r+1)>0, the reaction eigenvalues are ±ia​. This linear marginal case is a weakly attracting focus, not a nonlinear center. To check it directly, put u=(1+r)(1+x), v=(1+r)2(1+y), h=(1+a)/2, β=(1−a)/2, ω=a​, and X=x, Y=(hy−ax)/ω. The equations become X˙=−ωY+F2​+F3​+O(4), Y˙=ωX+G2​+G3​+O(4), with
F2​=(βX−ωY)2/h,F3​=−(aX+ωY)(βX−ωY)2/h2,G2​=ω(hX2−F2​),G3​=−ωF3​.
(48)
On the unit circle write A=cosθF2​+sinθG2​, B=cosθF3​+sinθG3​, C=cosθG2​−sinθF2​. In polar coordinates, dϱ/dθ=(A/ω)ϱ2+(B/ω−AC/ω2)ϱ3+O(ϱ4). The quadratic angular average vanishes. Integrating the quadratic correction over a whole cycle contributes its final squared integral, also zero, leaving the cubic average. Using the even trigonometric moments gives ⟨B⟩=a/4 and ⟨AC⟩/ω=(a+1)/8. The Poincaré map is therefore ϱ↦ϱ+[2π/ω](a−1)ϱ3/8+O(ϱ4). Since 0<a<1, it contracts sufficiently small positive radii and proves nonlinear asymptotic stability at the threshold.

Turing threshold of a basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model (kc2​=q/p​)

Words: 89
Basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model OurBigBook.com
Add diffusivities 1,p to the basally forced quadratic activator-inhibitor model. A Fourier mode with s=k2 has matrix J−sdiag(1,p) and determinant D(s)=ps2+(q−pa)s+q. When q>a, its trace is negative for every s≥0. A positive-growth mode therefore occurs precisely when D(s)<0 for some positive s. The parabola has a positive minimizer only if pa>q, and its minimum is negative exactly when (pa−q)2>4pq. Thus the ordinary Turing instability requires a>0, q>a and p>q/(1+a​−1)2. At onset, kc2​=(pa−q)/(2p)=q/p​ and the critical wavelength is 2π(p/q)1/4. A bounded spatial domain further requires an allowed mode inside the unstable band.

Inhibitor in a reaction-diffusion system

Words: 28
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
An inhibitor in an activator-inhibitor reaction–diffusion system suppresses the activator. Its diffusion and reaction feedback can stabilize a spatially uniform state while allowing some nonzero wavenumbers to grow through a Turing instability.

Activator in a reaction-diffusion system

Words: 41
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
An activator in an activator-inhibitor reaction–diffusion system is a species whose local feedback enhances activation. Near a homogeneous equilibrium, positive self-feedback is reflected in the corresponding diagonal entry of the reaction Jacobian matrix. Cross-coupling to an inhibitor and differing diffusion rates can generate a Turing instability.

Quadratic activator-inhibitor model (ut​=uxx​+u2/v−bu,vt​=dvxx​+u2−v)

Words: 166 Articles: 2
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
For positive concentrations and positive parameters, this reaction–diffusion system has homogeneous equilibrium (u∗​,v∗​)=(1/b,1/b2) and reaction Jacobian matrix (b2/b​−b2−1​). Its trace is b−1 and determinant is b, making the equilibrium reaction-stable exactly when 0<b<1. Stable complex eigenvalues permit damped oscillations, which must be distinguished from sustained periodic oscillations.

Turing threshold of the quadratic activator-inhibitor model (0<b<1,db>3+22​)

Words: 62
Quadratic activator-inhibitor model OurBigBook.com
A mode with squared wavenumber q in the quadratic activator-inhibitor model has negative trace b−1−(1+d)q when 0<b<1. Its determinant is D(q)=dq2+(1−db)q+b. A positive minimum location and a negative minimum require db>1 and (db−1)2>4db, equivalent to db>3+22​. At onset, the double determinant root is qc​=(1+2​)/d. In a bounded domain an admissible nonzero spatial mode must additionally lie in the open negative-determinant band.

Positive-quadrant Dulac multiplier for quadratic activation (∇⋅(u−2(f,g))=(b−1)/u2)

Words: 58
Quadratic activator-inhibitor model OurBigBook.com
For the diffusionless quadratic activator-inhibitor model, choose the Dulac function u−2. Then u−2f=1/v−b/u and u−2g=1−v/u2, giving divergence (b−1)/u2. For 0<b<1 it is strictly negative throughout the simply connected positive quadrant. Green's theorem rules out a periodic orbit: its boundary flux would be zero because the rescaled vector field is tangent to the orbit, while its interior divergence integral would be negative.

Spatially homogeneous equilibrium

Words: 36
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
A spatially homogeneous equilibrium of a reaction–diffusion system is a constant state u∗​ satisfying f(u∗​)=0. Since its spatial derivatives vanish, its stability to homogeneous perturbations is determined by the Jacobian matrix Df(u∗​); diffusion can additionally destabilize nonconstant modes.

Morphogen reaction-diffusion equation

Words: 71 Articles: 2
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
A morphogen reaction-diffusion equation models a spatial concentration by diffusion and local production or decay. Linearization at a homogeneous equilibrium C=0 replaces f(C) by f′(0)C.
It is a transport-and-reaction model for a morphogen, rather than the identity of the signaling molecule concept.

v(k)=1+k2u(k)​.

Turing pattern

Words: 210 Articles: 5
Reaction–diffusion system OurBigBook.com
A Turing pattern is a spatially structured state produced by interactions between local reactions and diffusion. A Turing instability explains linear pattern onset when a homogeneous equilibrium is stable without diffusion but unstable to a nonzero spatial mode.

Turing instability

Words: 176 Articles: 4
Turing pattern OurBigBook.com
A Turing, or diffusion-driven, instability occurs when a spatially homogeneous equilibrium is stable to homogeneous perturbations but unstable to a nonzero spatial Fourier mode after unequal diffusion is introduced.
Fast-inhibitor cubic activator growth rate (σ(k)=−r−Dk2+ρk2/(1+k2))
Words: 49
Turing instability OurBigBook.com
For ut​=Duxx​−u(u−r)(u−1)−ρ(v−u) and 0=vxx​−v+u, a Fourier mode perturbation about zero has v=u/(1+k2) and growth rate σ(k)=−r−Dk2+ρk2/(1+k2). If ρ>D, its maximum is −r+(ρ​−D​)2 at k2=ρ/D​−1; if ρ≤D, its maximum is −r at zero. Replacing (u,v,r) by (1−u,1−v,1−r) gives the corresponding criterion at the other homogeneous equilibrium.

Words: 39
Brusselator OurBigBook.com
The spatially homogeneous Brusselator has its unique positive equilibrium at (r,s/r). Its Jacobian there has determinant r2 and trace s−1−r2. If s−1>r2, the equilibrium is a repeller inside the Brusselator trapping region; the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem then supplies a periodic orbit.
